html:
Champa was a group of Cham kingdoms along the coast of central and southern Vietnam, from about the 2nd century CE until 1832. The Cham spoke an Austronesian language and grew from the seafaring Sa Huỳnh culture of the coast.

Chinese records name a kingdom called Linyi there from 192 CE, after a revolt against Han rule, though how it relates to later Champa is unclear. Scholars now think Champa was usually a loose federation of river-mouth states rather than one kingdom. Each lived from ports on the sea route between China and the Indian Ocean, trading aloeswood, ivory and other forest goods.

Hindu kings ruled it, and they built red brick temple towers to Shiva, the greatest group at Mỹ Sơn. Sanskrit and Cham inscriptions record their deeds. It also gave the world Champa rice, a fast-ripening rice that the Song dynasty took up in China.

Its history was one of long wars on two fronts:

  • With the Khmer: a Cham fleet sacked Angkor in 1177, and Jayavarman VII took revenge and ruled Champa for a time.
  • With Đại Việt to the north, which pushed south step by step in the "southward advance", or Nam tiến. The fall of the capital Vijaya in 1471 was the turning point.

The last Cham principality was annexed by the Nguyễn emperor Minh Mạng in 1832. Several hundred thousand Cham still live in Vietnam and Cambodia, most of them Muslim, with a Hindu minority.
sum: Champa was a group of Cham kingdoms along the coast of central and southern Vietnam, from about the 2nd century CE until 1832. The Cham spoke an Austronesian language and grew from the seafaring Sa Huỳnh culture of the coast.
